documents.title: New Patient Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Curtis is 20, here to set up primary care. Previously at a family practice near where he grew up; he is now in school locally and works some shifts at a store.

SICKLE CELL: HbSS, picked up at birth. Has an adult hematology clinic that took over from pediatrics. On hydroxyurea 1000 mg a day, which he admits he takes on and off the way hematology has framed it for him, plus folic acid 1 mg. Remembers being admitted as a teenager more than once with acute chest syndrome; cannot give dates. No pain episode needing the hospital this past year. Hematology writes his hydroxyurea; he would like us to handle everything else.

ASTHMA: since grade school. Uses albuterol a few times a month, more with colds or cold air. No night symptoms, no oral steroids in years, no ED visits for breathing. Needs a new inhaler script.

PSH: none. Allergies: none to medications.
Family: mom and dad both carry sickle trait. His father's mother has asthma. Nothing else he knows of.
Social: never smoked, no vaping. A drink once or twice a month. Lives with roommates during the semester. Full-time student, part-time retail.

ROS: no chest pain, no shortness of breath at rest, no fevers, no jaundice he has noticed beyond his usual yellow tint in the eyes when tired, no urinary symptoms, no leg ulcers, no vision change.

EXAM: thin young man, comfortable. Vitals per flowsheet. Mild scleral icterus. Mouth normal. Neck supple, no nodes. Heart RRR, soft systolic flow murmur at the left sternal border. Lungs clear, good air movement, no wheeze. Abdomen soft, nontender, no spleen tip felt, liver edge not enlarged. Legs without ulcers or swelling. Skin otherwise unremarkable. Mood and affect normal.

A/P
1. Sickle cell anemia, HbSS, on hydroxyurea via hematology. CBC with diff, retic count, CMP today; will send copies to his hematologist. Continue folic acid.
2. Mild intermittent asthma, controlled. Albuterol HFA renewed. Reviewed when to call.
3. Health maintenance: functionally asplenic, so pneumococcal coverage matters; PCV20 given today. HIV and hep C screening done today. Prior vaccine record requested. PHQ-2 negative.
4. Records release signed for prior office and hematology.
RTC one year, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Curtis, your blood work is back. Your hemoglobin and retic count sit where I would expect for HbSS, and your bilirubin is mildly up in the usual way for sickle cell. Kidney and liver numbers are fine. HIV and hepatitis C screens are negative. I faxed a copy to your hematology clinic. Nothing to change.

Records from prior family practice, 2009 through 2022, 41 pages.
Problem list: sickle cell anemia (HbSS), followed by pediatric then adult hematology; asthma, intermittent.
Hospital admissions for acute chest syndrome in adolescence are referenced in hematology correspondence; discharge summaries not included.
Immunizations: childhood series complete per state registry printout, including MenACWY, HPV series, and PPSV23 in childhood. Annual influenza most years.
Medications at last visit: hydroxyurea per hematology, folic acid 1 mg daily, albuterol inhaler as needed.
Allergies: NKDA.

Abstracted by RN: vaccine history entered; no screening gaps for age.

Adult Sickle Cell Program, outpatient follow-up. Visit date: 09/12/2023.

Dear colleague,
Thank you for sharing Mr. Chapman's June labs. He is a 21-year-old with HbSS seen today for routine follow-up. He has had no hospitalizations since last visit and manages occasional mild pain at home. We reviewed hydroxyurea; he takes it most days and we discussed the benefit of steadier use, but he prefers the current approach and we will revisit. Exam unremarkable apart from mild scleral icterus. Counts are at his steady state.

Plan: continue hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily. CBC with retic every 3 months, which can be drawn at your office if more convenient. Return here in 6 months.
Medications: hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, albuterol as needed.
Allergies: NKDA.

Sincerely,
Attending hematologist

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: pain under the right ribs after eating.
About three weeks of episodes, maybe five or six total, usually an hour or so after a heavy or greasy meal (pizza, fried food at work). Aching, right upper belly, lasts 1-2 hours, goes away on its own. Some nausea once, no vomiting. No fever, no dark urine beyond usual, no pale stools, no change in his eye color per him. Different from his sickle pain, which is legs and back.
Meds unchanged.

Exam: afebrile, vitals as charted. Mild icterus, his baseline. Abdomen soft, mild tenderness RUQ on deep palpation, no rebound, no mass, normal bowel sounds. Lungs clear.

A/P: postprandial RUQ pain in a young man with chronic hemolysis, classic for pigment stones until shown otherwise. RUQ ultrasound ordered. Low-fat meals meanwhile. If fever, constant pain or jaundice, go to the ED.

reports.text:
Indication: postprandial right upper quadrant pain; sickle cell disease.
The gallbladder contains multiple mobile echogenic shadowing stones. Gallbladder wall is not thickened. No pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic tenderness was not elicited. Common bile duct is normal in caliber. Liver is normal in size and echotexture without focal lesion. Visualized pancreas unremarkable. Right kidney without hydronephrosis.
reports.conclusion: Cholelithiasis without sonographic evidence of acute cholecystitis. Normal caliber common bile duct.

documents.title: Ultrasound result call

General Surgery Clinic, outpatient consultation. Date of service: 09/17/2024.
Reason: symptomatic gallstones, referred by his primary care office.

22-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS) and intermittent asthma, with recurrent postprandial biliary-type pain over the summer. Ultrasound in August shows multiple gallstones with a normal duct and no cholecystitis. No episodes of jaundice, pancreatitis or fever.
No prior operations or anesthetics he can recall. Medications: hydroxyurea, folic acid, albuterol as needed. NKDA.
Exam: abdomen soft, no tenderness today, no hernias.

Impression: symptomatic cholelithiasis.
Plan: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Risks, benefits and alternatives reviewed and he wishes to proceed. Scheduling for early November, after midterms, at his request. Pre-anesthesia evaluation per hospital protocol.

Thank you for the referral.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary, general surgery
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Department of Surgery. Admission 11/04/2024, discharge 11/07/2024.

Procedure: laparoscopic cholecystectomy (elective, for symptomatic cholelithiasis).

Hospital course: Approximately ten minutes after induction of general anesthesia the patient developed rapid breathing, tachycardia and masseter rigidity with limited mouth opening. Malignant hyperthermia was suspected and the hospital MH protocol was activated: the volatile agent was discontinued, the circuit changed, and IV dantrolene administered with prompt response. The operation was completed laparoscopically under total intravenous anesthesia without further event. He was transferred to the surgical ICU for monitoring, transferred to the floor on postoperative day 2 and advanced to a regular diet.

Discharge diagnoses: symptomatic cholelithiasis, status post laparoscopic cholecystectomy; intraoperative malignant hyperthermia crisis; sickle cell disease (HbSS); asthma.

Discharge instructions: he should be considered malignant hyperthermia susceptible for all future procedures; triggering agents (volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine) are to be avoided. Medical alert identification recommended. First-degree relatives should be informed. Resume home medications: hydroxyurea, folic acid, albuterol prn. Surgery clinic follow-up in two weeks.
Allergies at discharge: NKDA; MH-susceptible, avoid triggering anesthetics.

Copy to primary care.

documents.title: Anesthesia event record
documents.author: anesthesiology
documents.body: Anesthesia record summary, 11/04/2024. ASA III (sickle cell disease). Induction with IV agents and maintenance with an inhaled agent planned. Shortly after induction, rising minute ventilation and end-tidal CO2, sinus tachycardia and jaw rigidity were noted. Managed as malignant hyperthermia per protocol: trigger agent stopped, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen on a clean circuit, dantrolene IV given, active cooling measures prepared. Case continued with propofol-based TIVA. Extubated at the end of the case and transferred to ICU. Patient and family counseled regarding MH susceptibility; referral information for MH counseling provided.

documents.title: Office Visit: after surgery
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here after his laparoscopic cholecystectomy on 11/4. Hospital records requested, not yet received; history from Curtis and his discharge paperwork.
He was told that shortly after he was put to sleep his breathing and heart rate shot up and his jaw locked, that they treated it as malignant hyperthermia with a medicine through the IV, finished the operation with a different anesthetic, and kept him in the ICU. Home on 11/7. Incisions sore for a week, now fine. Eating normally, no more post-meal pain. No fever, no dark urine beyond usual, no muscle pain now.
Since then he asked his mom, who said her brother had a bad reaction to anesthesia years ago that the family always thought was this same thing. He had never heard that before.

Exam: well. Vitals as charted. Port sites clean and healed. Abdomen soft, nontender. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility after an intraoperative MH crisis 11/4. Added to problem list and an anesthesia-trigger alert entered on the allergy list (avoid volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine). Recommended a medical alert bracelet and to tell any dentist or surgeon before sedation. Explained it runs in families; suggested his mother and her relatives let their own doctors know, given the uncle's history. Family history updated.
2. S/p cholecystectomy, recovering well. Gallstones resolved.
3. HbSS, asthma: unchanged; continue current meds.
Will review hospital summary when it arrives.

Adult Sickle Cell Program. Clinic date 02/25/2025.

Dear Dr. (primary care),
Curtis returns for routine review. Interval history notable for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in November complicated by an intraoperative malignant hyperthermia reaction; he recovered fully and we have flagged MH susceptibility in our records. No pain admissions. He continues hydroxyurea most days and folic acid daily.
Exam: well, mild icterus, no hepatosplenomegaly, no leg ulcers.
Labs today at his steady state.

Allergies: NKDA. MH susceptible: avoid volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine.

With thanks,
Hematology attending

events.reason: left flank pain and blood in urine

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
Indication: left flank pain, gross hematuria, sickle cell disease.
Technique: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast, including excretory phase images.
Findings: Left kidney is normal in size. On excretory images, contrast extends from the calyx into a left renal papilla, forming a small cavity at the papillary tip, consistent with papillary necrosis. No renal or ureteral calculus. No hydronephrosis or perinephric fluid. Right kidney enhances and excretes normally with no papillary abnormality. Bladder unremarkable. Gallbladder surgically absent. Liver, pancreas and adrenals unremarkable. No free fluid. Bowel normal in caliber. No lymphadenopathy.
reports.conclusion: Findings of left renal papillary necrosis. No urolithiasis or obstruction.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED. Date of service 05/14/2025.

HPI: 22-year-old man with HbSS sickle cell disease and a history of malignant hyperthermia during surgery last year, here for two days of left-sided flank pain with visibly bloody urine. No injury, no recent heavy exertion. No fever, no dysuria. He is vague about family history and mentions his father has some kind of blood problem.
Meds: hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily (taken intermittently per hematology), albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h prn wheeze, folic acid 1 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA. MH susceptible.
Social: never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks per month; student and part-time retail.

Exam: T 37.2, BP 130/80, HR 88, RR 16. Uncomfortable but nontoxic. Mild tenderness over the left CVA. Abdomen soft, no guarding, no rebound. No suprapubic tenderness.

Results: Urinalysis negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrite, large blood, RBC too numerous to count, red cell casts seen on microscopy. Creatinine and BUN within normal range. CT abdomen/pelvis with excretory phase: left papillary necrosis, no stone, no obstruction.

ED course and impression: renal papillary necrosis, left, in the setting of sickle cell disease. Pain controlled with IV fluids and acetaminophen. Discharged home.
Instructions: drink plenty of fluids; acetaminophen for pain; avoid ibuprofen, naproxen and other NSAIDs; follow up with primary care within 1 week and inform hematology; return for fever, clots or inability to urinate, or worsening pain.

documents.title: ER visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Went to the ER wed night for pain in my left side and my pee was red. they did a CT and said it was papillary necrosis in my kidney from the sickle cell. said to see you this week or next. urine is lighter now.

documents.title: RE: ER visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks Curtis. Front desk will set up a visit for next week. Keep up the fluids, use acetaminophen only (no ibuprofen or naproxen), and let your hematology team know. If the bleeding gets heavy, you pass clots, can't pee, or get a fever, go back to the ER. We are requesting the ER record.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary, hematology
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Hematology inpatient service. Admitted 01/09/2026, discharged 01/16/2026.

Reason for admission: acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis.

History: 23-year-old man with HbSS, prior acute chest syndrome as a teenager, renal papillary necrosis of the left kidney in May 2025, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility after a reaction during cholecystectomy in 2024. Admitted with a typical pain crisis managed with IV fluids and IV analgesia.

Course: On hospital day 3 he developed new right flank pain with visibly bloody urine. He denied trauma, known kidney stones or urinary infections; his renal function has been stable at baseline. Exam: right costovertebral angle tenderness, afebrile, no suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis: gross hematuria with rare white cells, no casts. Hematocrit 22% on admission, 10% on day 3. Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis, no stones. Impression: recurrent renal papillary necrosis, now right-sided. He received 4 units of packed red cells over two days. Hematuria cleared over the following days and pain settled. Hematocrit 24% on the morning of discharge.

Discharge diagnoses: HbSS with vaso-occlusive crisis; renal papillary necrosis, right; acute fall in hematocrit, transfused.
Discharge medications: hydroxyurea 1000 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, albuterol HFA as needed. No NSAIDs.
Allergies: NKDA. MH susceptible: avoid volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine.
Family history: father and mother with sickle cell trait; maternal uncle with suspected malignant hyperthermia under anesthesia; paternal grandmother with asthma.
Social: never smoker, occasional alcohol, college student working part-time in retail.
Follow-up: primary care within 1 to 2 weeks with CBC; hematology clinic in 4 to 6 weeks.

documents.title: Family call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt's mother called (verbal consent on file from pt to speak with her). Curtis has been in the hospital since Friday with a sickle cell pain crisis and then had blood in his urine again, other side this time; he needed blood transfusions. Expected home in a few days. Asked her to have him book a follow-up with us within 1-2 weeks of discharge. Will request records.

documents.title: Office Visit: after hospitalization
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospitalized 1/9-1/16 for a sickle pain crisis. No discharge summary yet; history from Curtis, his discharge paperwork and his mother's call.
Per patient: pain crisis treated with IV meds; on the third day his right side started hurting and his urine went red. Told it was the kidney papilla problem again, other kidney. His blood count dropped a lot and he got several units of blood. Home since Friday. Urine has looked normal for 4 or 5 days. Pain gone. Tired but improving, back in class Monday. Taking hydroxyurea and folic acid; no ibuprofen.

Exam: vitals as charted, afebrile. Mild icterus, conjunctivae a little pale. Heart RRR, flow murmur. Lungs clear. No CVA tenderness. Abdomen soft.
CBC today: Hgb 8.1, Hct 24.3, essentially back near his usual.

A/P
1. Vaso-occlusive crisis, resolved.
2. Renal papillary necrosis, now right side as well as left last May. Hydration, NSAID avoidance reinforced.
3. Post-transfusion anemia check: Hct 24.3, acceptable. Copy to hematology; he sees them next month.
4. Records request for discharge summary.
